name: GlyNAC
lead: GlyNAC is a combination of two amino acids, glycine and N-acetylcysteine (NAC, a precursor of cysteine), that are the building blocks limiting the body's synthesis of the antioxidant tripeptide glutathione. It is sold over the counter as a dietary supplement and has been studied mainly as an intervention for age-related glutathione deficiency, oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction.[4][14]

The concept was developed by Rajagopal Sekhar and colleagues at Baylor College of Medicine, whose group has published most of the human work on it, beginning with an open-label trial in older people with HIV in 2020 and a pilot trial in older adults in 2021.[4][8][15] A randomized trial in older adults followed in 2023.[7] The researchers report improvements in glutathione levels, inflammation markers, insulin resistance, muscle strength, cognition and body composition.[4][7]

The published human trials are small, were largely run by one research group, and enrolled older adults rather than people seeking cosmetic changes. No study has examined effects on facial appearance, skin or other aesthetic outcomes, and reviews describe the evidence as promising but preliminary.[6][4][2]

Glutathione deficiency, oxidative stress, ageing markers

paras: GlyNAC is used as a longevity-oriented supplement. The rationale is that glutathione levels fall with age, partly because the amino acids glycine and cysteine become less available, and that supplying both together might restore glutathione and reduce oxidative stress.[4] Its use for appearance is indirect: it is discussed in longevity and anti-ageing contexts rather than as a cosmetic ingredient, and no trial has tested a cosmetic outcome.

Glutathione is built from glutamate, cysteine and glycine. Researchers propose that in older people cysteine and glycine are the limiting supplies, and that NAC provides cysteine while glycine supplies the second amino acid.[4] Restoring glutathione is hypothesised to lower oxidative stress, improve mitochondrial fuel oxidation and reduce inflammation.[4][6]

Glycine itself is a non-essential amino acid that the body makes from serine, is a major component of collagen, and acts as a neurotransmitter.[1] NAC is an acetylated form of cysteine that is also used as a mucolytic medicine.

Sekhar's group reported that older people have glutathione deficiency and elevated oxidative stress, and tested supplementation first in aged mice, then in people.[4][14] A 2022 mouse study from the group reported lengthened lifespan with GlyNAC.[16] Human trials followed in older adults with HIV (open-label, 2020), a pilot trial in older adults (2021) and a 24-week randomized trial (2023).[15][8][7] A separate group has run a randomized trial in healthy older adults on glutathione redox status and oxidative damage.[19]

Trial reports describe the combination as generally well tolerated over the study periods, and a review of glutathione precursor approaches in HIV describes consistent safety signals.[4][5] Gastrointestinal effects are the usual concern with NAC. Long-term safety at the doses used in trials has not been established by published studies.

A 2021 open-label pilot trial in older adults reported that GlyNAC supplementation corrected glutathione deficiency and was associated with improvements in markers of oxidative stress, mitochondrial function, inflammation, insulin resistance, endothelial function, muscle strength and cognition.[8] An earlier open-label trial in older people with HIV reported similar patterns.[15]

A randomized clinical trial in older adults, published in 2023, reported that GlyNAC compared with placebo improved glutathione deficiency, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, inflammation, physical function and ageing hallmarks.[7] The authors have summarised their program in a 2021 review.[4] A pilot study in people with type 2 diabetes reported improved mitochondrial fuel oxidation and lower insulin resistance.[17]

A separate randomized controlled trial in healthy older adults examined glutathione redox status and oxidative damage with glycine and NAC supplementation.[19] Reviews note that the findings on NAC are context-dependent, with benefits in people with low baseline glutathione and inconsistent results in healthy populations.[6] Registered trials include studies of glutathione-based supplementation in HIV, Alzheimer disease and post-surgical pain.[20][21][22]

Several reviews place GlyNAC among supplements with plausible benefits for muscle and physical function in ageing, while noting that independent replication and long-term data are limited.[2][6] Animal studies report effects in aged mice on brain function and lifespan.[16][12]
